speechtext: I should like to say a word or two in connection with one feature of the remarks of the hon. member for Victoria, Ontario (Mr. McNevin), that is, the sale of dairy cows in the United States. I do not think that business ought to be interfered with at all. There is no more treacherous or risky business than the handling of dairy cattle. I know of one man who has been coming here from the United States since 1917 in order to purchase dairy cows. He takes them to his farm near Watertown, and other United States dairymen come here to purchase cows. Last year this man spent $100,000 in one district. The cows he purchased were not necessarily all raised in that particular district. The dairymen may deal in cows on the side. Some of these men will go perhaps one or two hundred miles out of the district in order to buy cows to increase their herds or to have some for sale. The United States buyers come in, and they generally know where they can get a truck load of cows to take back. We have had this amount of money coming in to help relieve a surplus of dairy cows. If there were no market for these dairy cows, many farmers would not raise their heifer calves. They know they have a chance of getting rid of any good dairy cows that they might have. Every year they are raising heifer calves, and in that way not only keeping up their own herds but having a surplus for sale. I think that market should not be interfered with but rather encouraged because it has been of considerable benefit to the dairymen of the whole district.

I wish to ask the minister some questions with respect to the dehydration of potatoes and to show how it affects us in New Brunswick. I am aware that two orders in council were passed, one in December of last year and another one more recently, making an appropriation, I presume out of this vote, to extend the policy of providing additional dehydration equipment. During the last war a substantial amount of dehydration was carried on in New Brunswick, and it was associated with the manufacture of starch. I am told that that is the only economic way in which the dehydration of potatoes can be carried on, because the peelings of the potatoes and the washings contain all the elements that are required in the manufacture of starch, and I am told further that the manufacture of the starch will cover the whole cost of the dehydration process.
We are desirous of having a couple of plants established in New Brunswick. The advantages would be obvious. Ninety per cent of the weight of a potato is water. Therefore a freight on three dollar potatoes shipped to a point in Nova Scotia means a considerable loss entailed in freight, and if the dehydration plant is not run in connection with the manufacture of starch, that specific part of the product which would make starch, the peelings and the washings, goes down the sewer. That is not a profitable proposition; it is not an economic method.
There are people in New Brunswick who are willing to operate a dehydration plant for potatoes in conjunction with the starch industry, and I ask the minister if he will not see that arrangements are made for the establishment of two plants in that province for the dehydration of potatoes. There is no such plant in Prince Edward Island, and perhaps consideration might be given to establishing one there too.
I am satisfied from what I have learned, that if one or two dehydration plants were established in New Brunswick in connection with the starch factories at present established there, all that freight would be saved, and it would be the economic way to handle the product. I am told that during the last war there was a plant in Carleton county, New Brunswick, employing 150 hanjis. It is said that the product was not perhaps as good as it ought to have been, but scientific processes have advanced a long way since then, and I understand that a product of the proper quality can now be produced.
The provincial department of agriculture of New Brunswick has been in communication with the minister and is asking for this. It would not be a large expenditure, and since we have had very little war work down in New Brunswick I would urge the minister to give serious consideration to appropriating $50,000 to establish two plants in New Brunswick for the dehydration of potatoes. There are men there who are willing to erect the buildings and do everything else that is necessary if this grant be made, and it might be returned to the department out of the profits.
I am making this plea on behalf of the New Brunswick potato producers. They have at times a surplus of potatoes. There may not be a surplus this year, but in three out of four years they have a surplus and this is one way in which they could utilize their surplus product. The suggestion I am making is the economic way of handling the situation
War Appropriation-Agriculture

with respect to potatoes. I am not speaking with regard to other vegetables at all. I have no plea to make for them. They can continue to be dehydrated in the plants already established in Nova Scotia; but with respect to potatoes I think plants ought to be established near starch factories, because this would not only mean a substantial saving in freight rates but a saving in the peelings and washings which could be converted into starch and which now go down the sewer. That is the way in which the matter is represented to me, and it seems to me to be a reasonable proposal. I hope the minister will give it his favourable consideration. Is it not true that the provincial department of agriculture have asked for this? Is it not true that they have pointed out the economic value of such a proposal? If they have, I just wish to supplement their representations to the minister with my own.

The committee will
realize, of course, that the discussion in connection with dehydration should properly take place under one of the previous items, but I think it is quite proper that I should answer now the question put by the leader of the opposition.
The matter does not come under the special products board, which was set up for the purpose of making arrangements with Britain with regard to any products other than those which come under the dairy products board or the bacon board. It has to do with eggs, for example, and other products of that kind.
It is true that the government of New Brunswick have made representations along the lines just stated by the leader of the opposition. One of the members of that government, as the leader of the opposition knows, is one of the big producers in that province and probably knows as much about the matter as anyone else there. The hon. member for Victoria-Carleton (Mr. Hatfield) is also quite a producer in that area, and I think he too will agree with everything that has just been said by the leader of the opposition.
The representations made are as has just been stated by the leader of the opposition, that if the dehydration process is carried on at a place where there is not a plant which is producing starch, this adds greatly to the cost of the dehydration. In other words, one has to be more careful about the peelings in order to get the full value out of the potato. But when the dehydration is done in conjunction with the making of starch, the peelings can be of any thickness desired, in order to make sure that the rest of the product is pure potato for making the dehydrated product.

Yes; that also is involved. In other words, the cost is pretty well taken care of by using the outer part of the potato for starch. That is the representation made to us, and any investigations and inquiries we are making with regard to the placing of any dehydration plant for vegetables in New Brunswick are in relation to establishing a plant for dehydrating potatoes in relation to the plants already there. If anything is done, I can assure the leader of the opposition that an effort will be made to have the first developments take place where there are starch-producing plants in order to get exactly the results which he has indicated.
I would point out, however, what was pointed out by the hon. member for Yale (Mr. Stirling), last night, and what I emphasized later, that this plan is still in the experimental stage. We have had discussions with the representative of the British food ministry with regard to the whole matter. The British government are establishing dehydration plants on the same plan in Great Britain and hope to make use of them before coming to us for our products. We are following along the line which the hon. member for Lethbridge suggested last night, of trying to see ahead tc what might be expected from this country ir potatoes and other products that might require dehydration. Up to the moment we have nc orders, and we have no assurance from Britaii that we shall have orders; but we are confident that the establishment of some of these dehydration plants, particularly those that can be operated in association with other plants such as the starch plants in New Brunswick, is required and would be of assistance in connection with the war, and if not, that they would still be of benefit in' dealing with the surpluses which we have occasionally in times of peace. Any assistance we give in that direction in that area, if the development leads to an increase in the number of plants, wall be made just along the lines suggested.

subtopic: PROVISION FOR GRANTING TO HIS MAJESTY AID FOR NATIONAL DEFENCE AND SECURITY
speechtext: I am content with that.

subtopic: PROVISION FOR GRANTING TO HIS MAJESTY AID FOR NATIONAL DEFENCE AND SECURITY
speechtext:
I am glad to have the
assurance of the minister that New Brunswick is receiving attention with regard to dehydration plants. During the last war I had a lot of experience in the dehydration of vegetables, both potatoes and turnips. I was interested in a company which dehydrated practically 90 per cent of the potatoes and turnips which were dehydrated during the last war. For the most part the quality of the goods proved

War Appropriation-Agriculture
satisfactory, especially' to the French government, for whom we manufactured a vegetable soup mixture.
What has been done to meet the shortage of milk cans? We have in my constituency a cheese factory, but we cannot secure milk cans for conveying milk to the factory. Has anything been done toward the securing of cans?

subtopic: PROVISION FOR GRANTING TO HIS MAJESTY AID FOR NATIONAL DEFENCE AND SECURITY
speechtext:
With regard to the
manufacture of milk cans, it is, of course, a priority matter which has to be dealt with by the priorities people. They have given to the production of milk cans what we think is a liberal amount of the requisite materials. It may not be as much as could be used, but still, as compared with other uses that are made of the same materials, we consider it is a liberal pi-ovision.
Some attempts were made to bring old cans back into use for the purposes for which they were intended. It has been found that milk cans are piled up almost anywhere and used for almost any purpose. Hundreds of them were brought back in compliance with a regulation which compelled people to return cans which were owned by the people who were presumed to be using them, and many cans were uncovered in various places. One official told me the other day that dozens of cans were found piled up behind one building last winter, and frozen in the ice. They had to chop the ice away in order to get the cans out for use at a time when there was a shortage of cans in many' parts of the country. Efforts are being made to utilize all of the old cans which can be found and put into condition to be used. An effort through priorities is also being made to have a proper number of cans manufactured.

subtopic: PROVISION FOR GRANTING TO HIS MAJESTY AID FOR NATIONAL DEFENCE AND SECURITY
speechtext:
We have had cans on
order for over four months, and have not received a can, and the manufacturers tell us that they cannot secure any material.

speechtext:

speechtext: It really does not come under this. Properly it would come under my general estimates.

speechtext:
Perhaps the minister
will be good enough to answer the question.

subtopic: PROVISION FOR GRANTING TO HIS MAJESTY AID FOR NATIONAL DEFENCE AND SECURITY
speechtext:
Yes, if it is not too
long.

speechtext:
Will the minister tell
us what does come under this item.

subtopic: PROVISION FOR GRANTING TO HIS MAJESTY AID FOR NATIONAL DEFENCE AND SECURITY
speechtext: Eggs, principally.

subtopic: PROVISION FOR GRANTING TO HIS MAJESTY AID FOR NATIONAL DEFENCE AND SECURITY
speechtext: I have received several complaints from Nova Scotia with respect to the regulations laid down a year ago with regard to the marketing of wool. I made inquiries from Mr. Dick, the wool administrator, who referred me to the wool board, and I have not heard anything from them, but he did advise me that the regulations came under the purview of the Department of Agriculture. The complaint is that prior to the enactment of these regulations the wool was gathered by agents from the farmers, and that all of the wool was marketed in that way. In addition to that, the farmer had the privilege of selling direct to the factories. Since the regulations were enacted, all of the wool has to be marketed through regular grading centres. The farmers complain that they are receiving less money now for their wool graded in that way than they were prior to these centres being set up, when it was taken direct from the farmer. It is necessary at times to ship the farmers' wool as far as three hundred miles, and the result is going to be that probably 50 per cent of the wool will be left on the farms. I do not know anything about the matter; that is the information I get from men who are engaged in this work. Would the minister enlighten us as to what the regulations are, how many centres are set up in that province, and what is the price now compared with the price prior to the enactment of the regulations?

subtopic: PROVISION FOR GRANTING TO HIS MAJESTY AID FOR NATIONAL DEFENCE AND SECURITY
speechtext:
As regards the last question, I think I can answer it by saying that there is very little comparison between the price now and the price previously, because the price previously was pretty much a prewar price, and of course the price of wool jumped rapidly after war was declared. I believe it was the first product which was put under control by the government, because of the demand for it for making uniforms and other clothing necessary for war purposes, which resulted in a rapid rise in price.
As far as the other matter is concerned, I think it could be much more effectively discussed under my general estimates, because of the fact that I have not the information here with regard to it. It is an item in the estimates having to do with grading, and really comes under the regular estimates, and if the suggestion meets with the approval of the hon. member I would prefer to leave the matter until that time.

The next

TVar Appropriation-Agriculture
speakername: @Acting Chair(man)? of Committees of the Whole

subtopic: PROVISION FOR GRANTING TO HIS MAJESTY AID FOR NATIONAL DEFENCE AND SECURITY
speechtext: Would the minister explain just what is being done with regard to assistance in the movement of grain both east and west?

subtopic: PROVISION FOR GRANTING TO HIS MAJESTY AID FOR NATIONAL DEFENCE AND SECURITY
speechtext: The arrangement relates to grains that are used for feed, and it includes wheat as well as coarse grains, and corn going west, not going east; corn going west from Manitoba to British Columbia, for example, but not corn coming east. All mill feeds are included as well. We are paying the freight from Fort William east to points in all of the provinces east; and on grains going west we are paying freight from Calgary and Edmonton west into British Columbia to be used for feeding purposes. Those payments up to date amount to about $5,000,000. We estimated that they would cost us about $6,000,000 throughout the year, but up to date we have paid out about $5,000,000. In short that is what is happening.

subtopic: PROVISION FOR GRANTING TO HIS MAJESTY AID FOR NATIONAL DEFENCE AND SECURITY
speechtext: Well, it is mill feeds, coarse grains going west? What grades are included? Is anything being paid on low grade wheat?

subtopic: PROVISION FOR GRANTING TO HIS MAJESTY AID FOR NATIONAL DEFENCE AND SECURITY

subtopic: PROVISION FOR GRANTING TO HIS MAJESTY AID FOR NATIONAL DEFENCE AND SECURITY
speechtext: Has the minister had complaints from poultry feeders and others in British Columbia regarding the prices they are paying for this grain, as to whether they are getting the advantage of this bonus or not? When I was out west in December I heard complaints, but I did not receive any specific proposals or suggestions. I wondered if complaints had been made; if so, what was in them, and what had been done.

We have had no complaints at all of just the nature that is suggested. We have had complaints arising from misunderstandings with regard to what freight rate was going to be deducted. There is a special order known as tariff 145 under the transport board, the old railway board, which by reason of representations made by the hon. member for New Westminster (Mr. Reid) over quite a number of years resulted in a reduction in the rate on grains that were being sold for feeding purposes in British Columbia. When we put the regulations into effect covering British Columbia we provided that that was the freight rate we were to pay wherever it was applicable. The suggestion has been made that some people have been preventing that from going into operation, as w'as intended, to the disadvantage of some
[The Acting Chairman.]
others, and we have been correcting the situation from time to time. I think it is working satisfactorily now.

speechtext: As I understand the position in reference to fertilizers, this is for the production of fats, to which the minister has referred, to be devoted to the war effort, and it has no relation whatever to assistance to farmers in the production of other crops.

item is "auditor general's office".
speakername: @Acting Chair(man)? of Committees of the Whole

speakerposition: Minister of Finance and Receiver General
speechtext: The items of the finance estimates are: first, the auditor general-
Shall we take them seriatim?
speakername: @Acting Chair(man)? of Committees of the Whole

speakerposition: Minister of Finance and Receiver General
speechtext: I think that would be best.

speakerposition: Minister of Finance and Receiver General
speechtext:
The auditor general conducts post audits, not pre-audits. He has a comparatively small staff, between three and four hundred. I think to be exact it is 357. That staff of course does not compare in size with the staff of the comptroller of the treasury. The comptroller of the treasury pays the bills that are due from the government. The staff there is very large. I could not say the number offhand, but I think the temporary staff is between 3,000 and 4,000.
War Appropriation-Finance

The auditors that the hon. gentleman has spoken of as being in the various departments are employees of the comptroller of the treasury. His responsibility is very great; for it is he who makes sure that the amounts are due and payable, that they are authorized by some statute or vote of this parliament, and that the proper allotment has been made. All that must bo ascertained before the accounts are paid.
There are no auditors so far as I know who are responsible to the various ministers other than the Minister of Finance. There may be some exceptions to that; I think one is that the Department of Munitions and Supply act as agent for the United Kingdom government in purchasing and making payments in this country, and that department has a certain financial staff of its own which is engaged in this work which it has undertaken on behalf of the United Kingdom government. I do not think there are any other exceptions, but if so they are insignificant. The cost accountants and auditors and so forth are members of the staff of the comptroller of the treasury.
The auditor general as an officer of this parliament, responsible to this parliament, comes along afterwards and makes test audits here and there, checking three things: first, that there is a vote that is authority for the payment of the money; second, that there is a proper allocation out of which the money can be applied to the purpose to which it has been applied; and third, that the facts justify the payment. That is the system of audit of payments in this country, putting it very generally.

I think I raised this question once when I discovered a certain order in council. The minister will agree with me in this general statement, that the underlying principles of the Consolidated Revenue and Audit Act have been largely set aside for war purposes, owing to the exigencies of the occasion. A new system has to a degree supplanted what was intended by the audit act passed in the early thirties, and which was intended to be a safeguard of public expenditure. The audit act was modelled with great care. The present auditor general was then, I think, the comptroller of the treasury.
I remember the matter being referred to the banking and commerce committee, and we went into it with great care. It was intended to plug up some of the holes that had been found in the old system with respect to expenditures by departments without a vote of parliament. The minister has explained that it was necessary to set up a new system to take care of the present situation. I have been 
content with that all along, but I should like to have his assurance that the greatest care is being exercised in the checking of accounts before they are paid.
There is the question of cost-plus contracts. Per se I have no objection to cost-plus contracts. They operate well if everyone is honest. The danger is that all people are not honest in working out cost-plus contracts. I am content for my own part-I am not speaking for anyone else-to let it go without any further discussion, on the theory that the minister and his officials are watching the matter carefully. If we find that the system does not work, or if there are abuses, then I think the position will have to be reviewed.

speakerposition: Minister of Finance and Receiver General
speechtext: Yes. The section of the Consolidated Revenue and Audit Act to which the hon. gentleman refers-I am not sure of the number-is a very important section. But it proved to be unworkable under war conditions. In the fall of 1940 the Department of Finance did considerable work in devising a change in the system which would enable war business to be proceeded with. There is an order in council-

Passed
under the War Measures Act.

speakerposition: Minister of Finance and Receiver General
speechtext:
Yes, passed I think oil
November 19, 1940, effecting an amendment to that vital and important section. But I think that no exception can be taken to the order in council on the merits. The exception that was taken on one occasion was that we should have come to parliament for such an important change; that was debated here.
Parliament was in session then, in November, 1940.

speakerposition: Minister of Finance and Receiver General
speechtext: Yes. The new plan was worked out in September and October. The order was drawn and redrawn, suggestions made and further changes, and a tremendous amount of work put on it. I think it is a very workable order and that it adequately protects the treasury. The objections that I get are not that amounts are paid without adequate investigation, but the reverse-that accounts are delayed; that the comptroller of the treasury is obliged to make such careful investigation that persons dealing with (he government do not get their money as soon as they should.
That is because of congestion of business, I expect.

speakerposition: Minister of Finance and Receiver General
speechtext: Yes, very largely.

I want to place this
responsibility. There are twenty-five of these

War Appropriation-Finance
boards expending money without the authority of parliament, ultra vires. I read from the auditor general's report, for year ended March 31, 1941, page 541:
There are approximately twenty-five statutory or corporate bodies performing administrative functions.
He includes as corporations the Department of Munitions and Supply and several others.
He says:
In some instances the exercise of financial control is similar to that applied to expenditures of a department under a minister. . . .
But notice these words:
. . . but the terms of some acts are of such a nature as to vest final responsibility in the corporate management. The various acts stipulate whether the audit of accounts is to be by the auditor general or by commercial auditors. With the growth of this means of administration, it may be in the public interest to establish a practice whereby any qualification in an audit certificate may be promptly investigated and a procedure provided whereby expenditures may be recovered when an ultra vires payment is established.
That is the practice in New Zealand in connection with corporations and boards corresponding to our Department of Munitions and Supply, for example. In New Zealand it is provided by legislation that these corporations have to account to parliament for their expenditures; and if payments are made ultra vires of their authority a great deal of the money can be recovered. That is what should be done here, where we are paying out hundreds of millions of dollars.
I should like to refer to the travelling expenses of these non-salaried officers, the dollar-a-year men, which are referred to at page 540 of the auditor general's report. He directs attention to the fact that many of these payments are illegal. That places an onus on me as a member of parliament; but now, having done my duty in bringing the matter to the attention of the house, I am absolved of any responsibility. We have hundreds of these men whose travelling expenses are being paid. They are running all over the continent of north America, giving lectures and all the rest of it. In this regard the auditor general states:
The status of those who serve without remuneration is indefinite for executive travel regulations purposes. The audit disclosed cases of travel expenses being paid, although the records do not establish that the individual holds any public appointment.
They have no authority at all; they are not acting as agents of parliament, and the auditor general calls the situation to our attention.
Here we are in the seventy-eighth day of the
session, yet we have never had a chance to say a word about it.
The trend of policy now is to have such individuals certified as appointed without remuneration. More generally, appointments without salary are made by an executive order which stipulates, as a rule, a per diem allowance which may be claimed in lieu of a detailed accounting for subsistence and shelter. But eases were noted of accountings being made without employing the permissive per diem rates. Neither departments nor the treasury insisted on non-salaried officers submitting claims in the detail required from salaried officers. Likewise, the standards of travel to be observed by salaried officers were not strictly applied to those who serve without remuneration.
Then he goes on to refer to some matters in detail. No doubt we have a good auditor general; he has served under very fine ministers, but there is no public control over the great amount of money we are spending and we refuse to back him up and veto it. I can tell you that money is being wasted all over Canada, with absolutely no control and no report made to parliament. I am dealing with an important matter, which directly affects the navy department, and I think I should have the attention of the minister of that department, as well as the attention of others in the committee, to whom I am speaking. I should like to have order. I am not raising this question for fun, and I do not wish to be interrupted. I have brought up matters in the house relating to the navy, with regard to expenditures, and I have been unable to get proper replies from the minister. I object to this being treated as a trivial matter. We have appointed an auditor general, a good man who has done his duty. Would that we had an auditor general like Mr. McDougall; such is needed to-day.
I object to the way the business of the country is being conducted. I can only add this, that now I have brought the report of the auditor general, and the illegal expenditures that have been made, to the attention of parliament, I have done my duty. The last time the estimates were under consideration I also raised this question, and pointed out that we have no control over these expenditures. I can tell you this, that in many cases We have no audit at all. Even if we have an audit which is not satisfactory, the taxpayer is not protected. Some of these contracts are not carried out properly, and in my opinion something should be done about it. We have in the house many hon. members representing the farmers. Do they know of any private corporation that could vote money
Questions

like this, and stay in business? Here we are spending a mint of money without proper control; the country is suffering; the minister is proposing to impose income taxes and various other taxes on the poor people; the men running our retail stores are being put out of business. The other day the chairman of one of our boards said the competitive end of any business was through for the duration of the war, and after the w'ar is over these bureaucratic boards will continue to spend money like water and just snap their fingers at the high court of parliament. We might just as well go home if we are to have this expenditure of public money in this way, without any public control. How are the war expenditures dealt with? Well, we have the report of the auditor general; we know how that is done. I object to these expenditures, Mr. Chairman. I have raised the question, as I did last session, and having done so I have done my duty.
Progress reported.
